title: Cheapest Order to Saw a Plank
statement:
A plank is n units long, with marks at positions 0 to n. You must saw it at every position listed in cuts, one cut at a time, in any order you like.

Sawing a piece costs the current length of that piece, not of the original plank. After a cut, the piece falls apart into two pieces and later cuts only touch the piece that contains them.

Return the smallest possible total cost of making all the cuts. cuts is not necessarily sorted.

examples.why: Cut at 5 first (cost 10). Then cut 2 inside the 0–5 piece (cost 5) and 7 inside the 5–10 piece (cost 5). Cutting in the listed order costs 10 + 8 + 5 = 23.
Cut at 3 (cost 9), then 1 inside 0–3 (cost 3), then 6 inside 3–9 (cost 6).
One cut on the whole plank costs its full length.

hints: Greedy rules like 'cut nearest the middle first' fail. Think about what the first cut does: it splits the problem into two independent ones.
Sort the cuts and add the ends 0 and n. Let cost(i, j) be the cheapest way to make all cuts strictly between marks p[i] and p[j]. Which cut goes first inside that piece?
cost(i, j) = (p[j] − p[i]) + min over i < m < j of cost(i, m) + cost(m, j), and 0 when no cut lies between. Fill it by increasing gap j − i.

explain.intuition:
Whatever piece you are looking at, the first cut inside it costs the piece's full length, no matter which cut you choose. After that, the left part and the right part never interact again. So the cost of a piece is its length plus the best way to split it in two, and that is a recursion over pieces.

The pieces that can ever appear are exactly the ranges between two cut positions (or the ends). Sort the cuts, put 0 and n around them, and index pieces by pairs of positions (i, j). With m cuts there are about m²/2 pieces and each tries up to m first cuts, so it is O(m³). It does not depend on n at all, which is why a 10⁶-long plank is no problem.
steps: Sort cuts and build p = [0, ...cuts, n]; let k = p.length.
Let dp[i][j] be the cheapest cost for the piece from p[i] to p[j]. Neighbors (j = i + 1) cost 0.
For gaps 2, 3, … up to k − 1, and every i: try each m between, and set dp[i][j] = p[j] − p[i] + min(dp[i][m] + dp[m][j]).
pitfalls: Forgetting to sort cuts. Pieces are ranges of positions, so the DP needs them in order.
Paying the original length n for every cut instead of the current piece's length.
Indexing the DP by plank positions (size n × n). With n = 10⁶ that is far too big; index by cut indexes.

solutions.title: Try every first cut, no memo
solutions.idea: For a piece, try each cut inside it as the first one and recurse on both sides. Correct, but the same pieces are solved again and again.

solutions.title: Interval DP over sorted cut positions
solutions.idea: Sort the cuts, add both ends, and fill dp[i][j] by increasing gap: the piece's length plus the best split point inside it.

followups: Return the order of cuts too, not just the cost.
Knuth's optimization makes this O(m²). What property of the best split point does it rely on?
